name: ACCG-2671

lead: ACCG-2671 is an experimental oral amylin receptor agonist being developed for obesity. The appearance payoff people follow it for is fat loss and a leaner body from eating less.

Amylin agonists act on satiety pathways, so the chain is activation of the amylin receptor, greater fullness, then lower intake and weight loss. Its only public record is a first-in-human phase 1/2 trial registration covering safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and the effect of food; no results have been published.

paras: It is described as a small-molecule pill taken by mouth, and access is limited to the clinical trial. Pipeline watchers track it as a possible oral alternative to injectable weight-loss drugs.
Safety and tolerability are the subject of the ongoing first-in-human trial, and no data are public. It is not approved for any use.

angle.text: ACCG-2671 is an early oral amylin agonist for obesity that fat-loss followers track as a possible pill route to a leaner body. It is meant to raise fullness so you eat less and lose weight. Its only public record is a first-in-human trial registration.

lead: ACCG-2671 is an investigational oral small-molecule amylin receptor agonist being studied for obesity. The aim of amylin-based drugs is fat loss: amylin is a hormone that increases fullness and slows stomach emptying, so a drug that acts like it is intended to reduce appetite and body weight, which people pursue for a leaner physique.[1][2]

The only public record of ACCG-2671 is a registered first-in-human phase 1/2 trial examining its safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and the effect of food.[1] No results have been published. The oral route distinguishes it from the injectable amylin analogs, such as pramlintide, approved in 2005 for diabetes, and cagrilintide, a long-acting analog from Novo Nordisk in phase 3 trials in combination with semaglutide.[2]

paras: Amylin is a 37-amino-acid hormone released with insulin from pancreatic beta cells. It slows stomach emptying, increases fullness, reduces post-meal glucose rises and suppresses food intake, largely via the brainstem's area postrema.[2] Pramlintide, a synthetic analog, was approved in 2005 for people with diabetes and is injected before meals; cagrilintide is proposed as part of CagriSema with semaglutide for type 2 diabetes and obesity.[2]

One trial is registered (NCT07815678), a phase 1/2 first-in-human study of safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and food effect in 164 participants with obesity. It began recruiting in late December 2025.[1] No results have been published.

timeline.event: Pramlintide, a synthetic amylin analog, approved for diabetes.[2]
